title: Student dropout prediction
description: Risk model that estimates each student's dropout probability and ranks the tutoring list: who to intervene with first when resources are limited. Pilot (POC) on the UCI dataset, with the decision threshold as a business dial.

problem.title: The Problem
problem.intro: Tutoring resources are limited: you cannot intervene with every student at once. The question is not just who is at risk, but who to intervene with first and how early.
items: Minority and imbalanced class (32% dropout): accuracy alone is misleading
Bounded intervention window: the early model has less data but arrives in time
Every false positive is a wasted tutoring session on a student who was not going to drop out
Pilot on the public UCI dataset; real institution data is requested separately

phases.title: 1. Understand (EDA)
phases.description: Business hypotheses confronted against data before modeling.
items: Unpaid tuition: 86.6% dropout vs. 24.7% for those up to date
0 courses passed in 1st semester: 79.4% dropout
Macroeconomic context discarded (correlations ≈ 0)

phases.title: 2. Prepare
phases.description: Data quality audit and feature engineering.
items: Dataset with no nulls or duplicates (comes preprocessed)
1st semester pass ratio as a feature
Cleaning recipe documented to apply to the institution's real data

phases.title: 3. Model
phases.description: An honest ladder of models, from the naive baseline to the risk model.
items: Metric chosen before training: dropout-class recall (business decision)
Logistic regression (1st semester and full) vs. Random Forest
Operational threshold 0.53 optimized by F1

phases.title: 4. Decision and prioritized list
phases.description: The operational deliverable: the student list ranked by risk for the tutoring team.
items: Risk bands: 87.8% real dropout in 'High' vs. 10% in 'Low'
The early version is chosen despite lower recall: it arrives in time to intervene
Each tutoring investment is justified by visible per-row signals (tuition, scholarship, passed courses)

subsections.title: Why logistic regression and not Random Forest
subsections.description: Random Forest detects slightly more dropouts but with lower precision.
items: RF: recall 0.778, precision 0.786 vs. logistic 0.722 / 0.869
Nearly identical F1 (0.782 vs. 0.788)
Logistic regression is interpretable: readable coefficients for the tutoring team

subsections.title: The threshold as a business dial
subsections.description: The default threshold (0.5) is not always the best for the decision.
items: Raising it favors precision: fewer wasted tutoring sessions, more undetected dropouts
Lowering it favors recall: more coverage, more false positives
Optimizing F1: threshold 0.53 → precision 0.88, recall 0.72

subsections.title: Early vs. full version
subsections.description: The full version wins on every metric, but you have to wait a year.
items: Full: recall 0.722 and AUC 0.908
Early: 65.8% of dropouts detected in time to intervene
Choosing which to use is a business decision, not a technical one

items.label: Metric first:
items.text: accuracy alone is misleading: the naive baseline already has 68% without detecting a single dropout.

items.label: Converging signal:
items.text: logistic regression and Random Forest agree on the variables that matter (tuition, scholarship, 1st semester passes).

items.label: Business trade-off:
items.text: choosing the early version with lower recall, because it arrives in time to act, is not a technical decision.
